lessons.culture: In Cairo, clothes shops from Downtown's Talaat Harb Street to the malls call the fitting room "البروفة", from the English word "proof", and sizes are usually said in English letters. Staff bring other sizes without fuss, and saying something does not fit is never rude.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks you: "مقاسك كام؟" Answer that your size is large.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatical, but stiff and bookish; in a Cairo shop people just say the borrowed size, "لارج", "ميديم", "سمول".

exercises.tip: Sizes are borrowed English words: سمول، ميديم، لارج.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks you (you are a woman): "أخدمك بإيه؟" Say you want a dress.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal and written; in speech Cairenes say "عايز" for a man and "عايزة" for a woman.

exercises.tip: عايز is for a man, عايزة for a woman; both come before the thing wanted with no "a".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عايز _____ لو سمحت." English: I want a shirt, please.

too_formal.feedback: This is a made-up bookish description; the everyday word is simply "قميص".

exercises.tip: In Cairene the ق of قميص is a glottal stop: 2ameeS.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "ده _____ عليا أوي." English: This is too tight for me.

too_formal.feedback: Correct Modern Standard Arabic, but not how people talk in a shop; Cairo says "ده ضيّق عليا أوي".

exercises.tip: ضيّق is tight; the opposite for clothes is واسع (loose).

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "Can I try it on?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "ينفع" is the everyday Cairene way to ask if something is allowed or possible.

exercises.tip: ينفع means "is it allowed / does it work"; قاس (a2eesu) is to measure or try on.

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "Do you have a smaller size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but written-style; in speech "عندك" replaces "هل لديك".

exercises.tip: Ask a woman with the same words: عندك is said 3andek.

exercises.prompt: What do Cairenes call the fitting room?

too_formal.feedback: Understood, but a Cairene shop assistant would say "أوضة البروفة".

exercises.tip: أوضة is the Cairene word for room (owDa), البروفة is the try-on.

exercises.prompt: Which word do Cairenes use for sports shoes?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but a shop assistant would say "كوتشي".

exercises.tip: كوتشي is the everyday word for sneakers; جزمة is a shoe or boot in general.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "This is too big for me."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairo says "ده" and "أوي".

exercises.tip: أوي (awi) means "very" and comes at the end.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "Where's the fitting room?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "فين" is the everyday Cairene question word for where.

exercises.tip: فين can come at the end or the start of the question.

lessons.culture: Cairo shop assistants readily say "لايق عليك" (it suits you) and "ألف مبروك" when you choose something, and it is common to ask a friend or the seller for an opinion before buying. Saying "ربنا يبارك لك فيه" (may God bless it for you) after a purchase is a warm, everyday habit.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks you: "رأيك إيه في الفستان ده؟" Say it is very nice.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; in speech Cairenes say "حلو أوي".

exercises.tip: حلو (7elw) is nice, pretty and tasty; أوي intensifies it.

exercises.prompt: A seller asks: "اللون ده عجبك؟" Say yes, you liked it a lot.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but bookish; Cairo says "عجبني" in one word.

exercises.tip: عجبني means "it pleased me"; the thing liked is the subject, so it does not change.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عندك لون _____؟" English: Do you have another color?

too_formal.feedback: Correct in Standard Arabic, but Cairenes say "تاني" for other or again.

exercises.tip: تاني means both "another" and "again".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا بحب الألوان _____." English: I like light colors.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "بحب" is what people actually say instead of "أفضل".

exercises.tip: فاتح is light (of color), غامق is dark.

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "This color doesn't suit me."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairenes use "مش" for not, and "لايق عليا" for suits me.

exercises.tip: مش negates a word in Cairene; لايق (laye2) is the same word for a man and for a thing.

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "I haven't decided yet."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairene wraps the verb in "ما ... ش" and uses "لسه" for yet.

exercises.tip: ما ... ش is the Cairene not; لسه is yet or still.

exercises.prompt: Which words mean "nicer than"?

too_formal.feedback: Also correct, but the shop-floor comparison is "أحلى من".

exercises.tip: Comparison in Cairene: adjective on the pattern أفعل followed by من.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Just give me this one"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but stiff and a bit curt; "خلاص، هاتلي ده" is the natural way.

exercises.tip: خلاص here means "that's it, decided".

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "This one is nicer than that one."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; in Cairo both sides are just "ده".

exercises.tip: ده is used for this and for that; you point to tell them apart.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "Which is nicer, red or blue?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "أيهما ... أم" is bookish; Cairo says "أنهي" and "ولا".

exercises.tip: ولا (walla) means "or" in questions.

lessons.culture: Bargaining is expected at Khan el-Khalili, Ataba, Al-Muski and street markets, where "يا باشا" and "يا حاج" keep it friendly, while chain stores and malls with price tags usually do not haggle. Sellers often say "عشان خاطرك" (for your sake) when they lower a price.

exercises.prompt: A seller says: "ده بألفين جنيه." Say it is very expensive.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "غالي أوي" is what people say at a stall.

exercises.tip: غالي is expensive, رخيص is cheap.

exercises.prompt: You are the shopkeeper. A customer asks: "ينفع تنزل السعر؟" Agree to lower it a bit for him.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairo uses the future "ه" and "شوية".

exercises.tip: The future in Cairene is ه + verb: هنزلك (I will lower it for you).

exercises.prompt: Complete: "بكام _____؟" English: How much is this?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "هذا" is the written form; Cairo says "ده" for masculine and "دي" for feminine.

exercises.tip: ده for masculine things, دي for feminine, دول for plural.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "مش هينفع، _____." English: I can't, I'll lose money.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; the Cairene future is "هخسر".

exercises.tip: هخسر is future: I will lose.

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "Isn't there cheaper than this?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "مفيش" is the everyday way to say there isn't any.

exercises.tip: مفيش means "there isn't"; كده means "like this".

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "How much is the total?"

too_formal.feedback: Understood, but at the till Cairenes ask "الحساب كام؟".

exercises.tip: الحساب is the bill or total; كام is how much.

exercises.prompt: Which words mean "final price"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "آخر سعر" is what sellers say.

exercises.tip: آخر means last or final.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Ok, we agreed"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "ماشي" is the everyday Cairene ok.

exercises.tip: ماشي means okay, agreed.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "Can you lower the price?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "ينفع" starts the everyday request.

exercises.tip: ينفع + verb asks "is it possible to...".

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "I want a discount because I'm buying a lot."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairo says "عشان" for because and "كتير" for a lot.

exercises.tip: عشان means because or in order to; the present with ب is باشتري.

lessons.culture: Many Cairo shops will exchange an item within a few days if you have the receipt, but often will not refund, and small market stalls may display the sign "البضاعة المباعة لا ترد ولا تستبدل" (sold goods are neither returned nor exchanged). Politeness helps, so people say "معلش" and "متشكر على تعاونك" while sorting it out.

exercises.prompt: A shop assistant asks you: "معاك الفاتورة؟" Say yes, you have the receipt.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairenes say "معايا" (with me).

exercises.tip: معايا is with me; معاك is with you.

exercises.prompt: A shop assistant asks: "اشتريته إمتى؟" Say two days ago.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; in speech people say "من يومين".

exercises.tip: من + a time means "since / ago": من يومين, من أسبوع.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عايز _____ القميص ده." English: I want to return this shirt.

too_formal.feedback: Correct in Standard Arabic, but shops say "أرجّع" for returning goods.

exercises.tip: أرجّع follows عايز directly with no "that".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "ده مش _____ طلبته." English: This isn't what I ordered.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "الذي" is bookish; Cairo uses "اللي" for who, which and that.

exercises.tip: اللي is the one word for who, which and that.

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "There's a defect."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "فيه" is the everyday Cairene way to say there is.

exercises.tip: فيه means "there is"; مفيش means "there isn't".

exercises.prompt: Type in Cairene: "I don't have the receipt."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairo wraps "عندي" in "ما ... ش".

exercises.tip: ما + عندي + ش is the Cairene way to say I don't have.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I didn't like the color"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairene negates with "ما ... ش".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says "I want to exchange it for another one"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "أبدّل" is the everyday word for exchange.

exercises.tip: أبدّل (abaddel) is to swap or exchange.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "I want to exchange it for another one."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; Cairo says "واحد تاني".

exercises.tip: واحد تاني means another one.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words: "Can I exchange it for a bigger size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal; "ينفع" opens the everyday question.

exercises.tip: بـ before the new thing means "for" when exchanging.

challenge.title: A Shopping Trip in Khan el-Khalili
challenge.instructions: Write and act a shopping conversation of at least 10 lines. It must include asking for an item by size, discussing a color choice, asking the price, bargaining at least once, and a return or exchange with the receipt mentioned. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 6 and include both a masculine-address and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: An opening request using عايز or عايزة and a clothing item.
A size question using مقاسك كام؟ or مقاسِك كام؟
A color question or preference using اللون.
A price question using بكام or كام.
At least one bargaining line using ينفع تنزل السعر؟ or نزّلي شوية.
A final price line using آخر سعر.
A return or exchange line using أرجّع or أبدله.
A mention of the receipt using الفاتورة.
A closing thank-you or blessing such as تسلم إيدك or ربنا يكرمك.
